terms.definition: The main federal program for financing affordable rental housing. State agencies award the credits, investors buy them, and that equity pays for part of construction. In return the homes stay rent-restricted for at least 30 years.
terms.short: Low-Income Housing Tax Credit — the main federal program funding affordable rental housing. States award the credits each year; investors buy them, and that equity lets the project keep rents affordable for 30+ years.

source.name: 26 U.S.C. 42, Low-income housing credit, subsections (a) and (h)(6)

terms.definition: A census tract where at least 50% of households earn less than 60% of area median income, or where the poverty rate is at least 25%. HUD designates the tracts, and a LIHTC project in one qualifies for a 30% basis boost.
terms.short: Qualified Census Tract — a HUD-designated tract where at least 50% of households earn under 60% of AMI, or the poverty rate is at least 25%. LIHTC projects here qualify for a 30% basis boost.

terms.definition: An area HUD designates because construction, land and utility costs are high relative to area median income. A LIHTC project in one qualifies for a 30% basis boost.
terms.short: Difficult Development Area — a HUD-designated place where construction, land and utility costs are high relative to local incomes. LIHTC projects here qualify for a 30% basis boost.

terms.definition: Colorado's housing finance authority. It allocates federal and state housing tax credits under its Qualified Allocation Plan, issues tax-exempt bonds and makes loans for affordable housing.
terms.short: Colorado Housing and Finance Authority — the state agency that allocates federal LIHTC credits, issues bonds, makes first-mortgage loans, and funds affordable housing in Colorado.

terms.definition: The middle household income for a county or metro area, published each year by HUD. Programs set income eligibility and maximum rents as a percentage of it, such as 30%, 50%, 60% or 80% of AMI.
terms.short: Area Median Income — the middle household income for a county or metro, published yearly by HUD. Programs use percentages of AMI (like 60% AMI) to set who qualifies and the maximum rents.

terms.definition: The area a proposed development is expected to draw most of its renters from. A market study measures demand, competing homes and rents inside it.
terms.short: Primary Market Area — the area a proposed project will draw most renters from, usually defined by drive time, school district, or natural boundaries. The market study measures supply and demand inside it.

terms.definition: A study of the gap between the homes a community has and the homes its households need, now and in the future. It looks at population, incomes, existing homes and affordability to guide planning and investment.

terms.full: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
terms.definition: The federal housing department. It runs Section 8, CDBG and HOME, and publishes the income limits, Fair Market Rents, and QCT and DDA designations that LIHTC projects use.
terms.short: Department of Housing and Urban Development — the federal agency that runs Section 8, CDBG and HOME, and publishes the income limits, Fair Market Rents and tax credit designations other programs rely on.

terms.definition: The St. Louis Fed's free database of economic data, including interest rates, prices, jobs and housing. It lists about 853,000 series from 127 sources.
terms.short: Federal Reserve Economic Data — the St. Louis Fed's free public time-series database covering housing, prices, employment, and rates.

source.name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

terms.definition: The Bureau of Labor Statistics measure of how the prices urban consumers pay change over time, rent included. It is the usual gauge of inflation in rent and operating cost projections.
terms.short: Consumer Price Index — Bureau of Labor Statistics measure of inflation in the prices households pay for a representative basket of goods and rent.

terms.definition: HUD's yearly estimate of the 40th percentile gross rent, meaning rent plus utilities, for an area and bedroom size. It sets voucher payment standards and serves as a rent benchmark.
terms.short: Fair Market Rent — HUD's annual estimate of rent for a modest unit, by county and bedroom size. Used to set voucher payments and benchmark LIHTC rents.

terms.definition: A federal law that pushes banks to meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. It is a main reason banks invest in tax credit equity and affordable housing loans.

A federal bill to expand LIHTC, partly enacted in July 2025. Its 12% increase in 9% credit allocations and its lower 25% bond financing test are law. The rest, such as an automatic basis boost in rural and Tribal areas, is still pending in Congress.
terms.short: Affordable Housing Credit Improvement Act — federal LIHTC legislation, partly enacted: its 12% increase in 9% credit allocations and lower (25%) bond-financing test became law in July 2025; its remaining provisions (such as an automatic basis boost in rural and Tribal areas) are still pending in Congress.

source.name: 26 U.S.C. 42, Low-income housing credit, as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, section 70422

terms.definition: The state department that supports local governments. It houses the Division of Housing and the State Demography Office, and tracks local Prop 123 commitments.
terms.short: Department of Local Affairs — Colorado state agency that runs the Division of Housing, the State Demography Office, and tracks Prop 123 commitments.

terms.definition: A national database of federally subsidized rental properties, including LIHTC and Section 8. It is used to track expiring subsidies and find homes at risk of losing affordability.

Population counted for each single year of age instead of in age groups. Figures in this form from the State Demography Office and the Census Bureau are used to build age pyramids and project housing demand.
The benchmark overnight interest rate, based on borrowing secured by Treasury securities, that replaced LIBOR. Variable-rate construction and bridge loans are usually priced from it.

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, SOFR

terms.definition: The Census Bureau's ongoing survey of people, incomes and housing. It publishes 1-year estimates for areas of 65,000 people or more and 5-year estimates for all areas.
terms.short: American Community Survey — the Census Bureau's rolling survey. 1-year estimates for places 65,000+; 5-year averages for smaller places.

source.name: Census Bureau, When to use 1-year or 5-year estimates

terms.definition: HUD's custom tabulation of American Community Survey data showing housing problems, such as cost burden and overcrowding, by household income. Local governments use it to document housing need.
terms.short: Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy — HUD's custom ACS tabulation showing housing need at specific AMI bands. Cleanest public read on the gap by income tier.

terms.definition: A family of Bureau of Labor Statistics indexes that track the prices producers receive. The construction indexes for lumber, steel and concrete are used to follow building cost trends.
An unincorporated community the Census Bureau defines so that it can publish data for it. It has no local government of its own, so there is no city council or municipal staff to plan for it.
terms.short: Census Designated Place — an unincorporated community with Census data but no local government. Planning targets that lack a city council or municipal staff.

terms.definition: Everything it costs to build a project: land, construction, design and legal work, financing, reserves and developer fee.
terms.short: Total Development Cost — every dollar to build the project: land, construction, design, financing, reserves, and developer fee.

terms.definition: A tax-exempt bond a state or local government issues for a private project such as affordable housing. A building gets 4% credits outside the 9% competition when bonds finance at least 50% of the building and land, or at least 25% for a building placed in service after 2025 when bonds issued after 2025 finance at least 5%.
A Census Bureau program that combines federal, state and Census records into statistics on jobs, earnings and where workers live. Its LODES files are the source for commuting figures.

The plan a state housing agency must adopt under IRC §42 to say how it will award housing tax credits. CHFA's plan sets the threshold requirements, scoring and priorities for 9% LIHTC in Colorado. The current plan covers 2027–28.
terms.short: Qualified Allocation Plan — CHFA's rulebook for awarding 9% LIHTC: threshold requirements, scoring criteria and priorities (rural, preservation, opportunity, deeply affordable).

terms.definition: The loan amount divided by the property's appraised value. Lenders cap it so that some equity stands behind the loan, and the cap varies by loan program.
terms.short: Loan-to-Value — the ratio of mortgage debt to property value. Lenders cap it, and the cap varies by loan program.

terms.definition: The yearly rate of return at which the present value of all an investment's cash flows, tax credits included, comes to zero. Investors use it to compare tax credit equity with other uses of their money.
terms.short: Internal Rate of Return — the discount rate at which a project's cash flows sum to zero. Investors compare LIHTC equity returns against this benchmark.

terms.definition: A property's yearly income minus operating expenses, before loan payments. Lenders size the permanent loan from it: the project can carry the loan whose payments NOI covers with the required margin (see DSCR).
terms.short: Net Operating Income — annual rental income minus operating expenses, before debt payments. The main measure of whether a building covers its mortgage.

terms.definition: A statistical forecasting method that projects a series from its own past values and past errors. This site uses it to project tax credit equity prices with a confidence range.

A low-income census tract where long-term investment earns federal capital gains tax benefits under IRC §1400Z-2. Colorado's 126 zones from 2018 stay active through 2028. Treasury has approved 91 Colorado tracts for the next round, which opens to investment on Jan 1, 2027.
terms.short: Opportunity Zone — a federally designated low-income census tract where investors get capital gains tax benefits in exchange for long-term investment.

terms.definition: A federal credit worth 39% of a qualified investment in a low-income community, claimed over 7 years. The CDFI Fund runs it. It can sit beside LIHTC in a mixed-use project with commercial space.

source.name: 26 U.S.C. 45D, New markets tax credit, subsection (a)

terms.definition: A local tool that sets aside the growth in property tax revenue from a district to pay for redevelopment there. It can fill part of the financing gap for affordable housing. In Colorado, urban renewal authorities can use it (see URA).
terms.short: Tax Increment Financing — local public financing tool that diverts future property-tax growth from a defined district to pay for current redevelopment.

terms.definition: A nationwide EPA dataset that summarizes land use, transit access, walkability and jobs for each census block group. This site uses EPA's own National Walkability Index for the walkability score, computes a bikeability score from SLD intersection density, land-use mix and auto network density, and reports SLD's distance to the nearest transit stop (D4A) as a distance, not a score.
terms.short: EPA Smart Location Database — a national geodatabase scoring walkability, transit access, and built-environment characteristics by census block group.

terms.label: Walkability score
terms.definition: EPA's National Walkability Index for the site's census block group, rescaled from EPA's 1–20 scale to 0–100. EPA builds the index from national rankings of four Smart Location Database measures: intersection density (1/3), proximity to the nearest transit stop (1/3), employment and household mix (1/6) and employment mix (1/6). This site does not reweight it. EPA's categories are used as labels: Most walkable (index above 15.25), Above average (10.51–15.25), Below average (5.76–10.5) and Least walkable (5.75 or below). Because the index includes transit proximity, it overlaps the separate transit measure in the access score.

source.name: EPA, National Walkability Index methodology and user guide

terms.label: Bikeability score
terms.definition: A proxy score estimating how conducive an area is to cycling, derived from EPA Smart Location Database metrics: low auto-oriented network density (40% weight), land-use mix (30%), and pedestrian intersection density (30%). Higher scores indicate areas with less car-dependent infrastructure and more mixed-use development. This is a proxy — it does not measure actual bike lane presence.

source.name: This site's method, using EPA Smart Location Database measures

terms.label: Cap rate
terms.definition: A property's yearly net operating income divided by its value or cost. It lets a reader compare the income a project produces with the capital invested and spot a deal whose operating return may be too thin.
terms.short: Capitalization Rate — annual net operating income divided by project value or cost. It helps compare the income a property produces with the capital invested.

terms.label: Eligible basis
terms.definition: The part of development cost that counts toward federal housing tax credits. Land and certain other costs are excluded, so changing the eligible share changes the credit and equity estimate directly.
terms.short: The portion of project cost that may be used to calculate federal housing tax credits. Land, commercial space and certain other costs are excluded.

terms.label: Qualified basis
terms.definition: Eligible basis after the applicable fraction and any allowed basis boost are applied. The credit rate is applied to this amount, so it controls the estimated yearly tax credits.
terms.short: Eligible Basis after applying the applicable fraction and any allowed basis boost. The credit rate is applied to this amount.

terms.label: Applicable fraction
terms.definition: The smaller of a project's low-income share of units and its low-income share of floor space, under IRC §42(c)(1)(B). In a mixed-income project it sets how much eligible basis becomes qualified basis.
terms.short: Under IRC §42(c)(1)(B), the smaller of the low-income unit fraction or low-income floor-space fraction. It sets how much Eligible Basis qualifies for credits in a mixed-income project.

terms.label: Basis boost
terms.definition: An allowed increase in eligible basis that produces more housing tax credits without adding cost. IRC §42(d)(5)(B) lets a project in a QCT or DDA count 130% of its basis, a 30% boost, and a state agency can give other buildings the same boost.
terms.short: A 30% increase in eligible basis (to 130%), which raises the tax credits a project can claim. Automatic in QCTs and DDAs, or by state designation. Often decides whether a deal pencils.

terms.label: Developer fee
terms.definition: The payment to the sponsor for assembling, financing and delivering the project. Its size, and the part deferred and repaid from operations, affect both total development cost and the financing still needed at closing.
terms.short: Payment to the sponsor for assembling, financing, and delivering the project. Its size and any deferred portion (repaid from operations) affect both project cost and the closing gap.

terms.definition: The direct cost of physical construction: labor, materials, site work and installed building systems. They are usually the largest part of the budget, so a change in them quickly widens or closes the financing gap.
terms.short: Direct physical construction expenses for labor, materials, site work, and installed building systems. They are usually the largest part of the development budget.

terms.definition: Development costs outside physical construction, such as design, engineering, legal work, permits, financing and insurance. Some count toward tax credit basis and some do not, and all of them still need funding.
terms.short: Development expenses outside physical construction, including design, engineering, legal work, permits, financing, and insurance.

terms.label: Debt service
terms.definition: The principal and interest a project must pay on its loans in a year. Comparing it with net operating income shows whether the proposed mortgage is supportable and how much cushion is left if revenue falls.
terms.short: The principal and interest a project must pay on its loans during a year. Comparing it with NOI shows whether the mortgage is supportable.

terms.definition: The share of potential rent assumed lost because homes are empty or rent goes uncollected. A higher assumption lowers effective income, which lowers the mortgage the project can support.
terms.short: The share of potential rent assumed to be lost because units are empty or rent is not collected. A higher assumption lowers effective income.

terms.label: Replacement reserve
terms.definition: Money set aside each year for future major repairs and the replacement of building systems. It reduces the cash available for loan payments today and protects the property from large unfunded costs later.
terms.short: Money set aside each year for future major repairs and building-system replacement. It protects the property but reduces cash available for debt payments today.

terms.label: Credit price
terms.definition: The amount an investor pays for each dollar of housing tax credit. A small change in price, multiplied over ten years of credits, moves project equity by a large amount.
terms.short: The amount an investor pays for each dollar of housing tax credit. Small pricing changes can move project equity substantially over the ten-year credit stream.

terms.definition: The price investors pay for a stream of housing tax credits and the tax benefits that come with them. It is a market assumption, not a guaranteed offer, so the value chosen changes how much cash the credits are expected to raise.
terms.short: The investor price for a stream of housing tax credits and related tax benefits. It is a market assumption, not a guaranteed offer.

terms.label: Placed in service
terms.definition: The date a building is ready and available for people to live in. The ten-year credit period starts that year or, if the owner chooses, the next, and the date sets which income limit table applies.
terms.short: The date a building is ready and available for residential use. It starts the credit and compliance timelines and sets the applicable income-limit table.

terms.label: Compliance period
terms.definition: The first 15 taxable years in which a LIHTC building must meet federal affordability rules, under IRC §42(i)(1). A failure in this period can trigger recapture of credits. An extended use period then keeps rents restricted for at least 15 more years.
terms.short: The first 15 taxable years of federal LIHTC affordability requirements under IRC §42(i)(1); noncompliance can trigger credit recapture. An extended use period in the recorded LURA keeps rents affordable at least 15 more years.

source.name: 26 U.S.C. 42, Low-income housing credit, subsections (i)(1) and (h)(6)

terms.label: Extended use
terms.definition: The affordability period that continues after the 15-year compliance period, under IRC §42(h)(6). The recorded agreement restricts rents and tenant incomes for at least 30 years in total, and often longer.
terms.short: The affordability period continuing after initial compliance under IRC §42(h)(6). It generally keeps restrictions in place for at least 30 years in total.

terms.label: Gap financing
terms.definition: The funding still needed after tax credit equity and supportable debt are subtracted from total development cost. It has to come from grants, soft loans, deferred fees or other sources before the project can close.
terms.short: The dollars needed to close the difference between project cost and what private debt and tax credit equity will fund. Filled with soft debt, grants, or fee waivers; often the hardest dollars to secure.

terms.label: Amortization
terms.definition: The scheduled repayment of loan principal through regular payments. A longer amortization period lowers yearly debt service and can support a larger loan, but it leaves principal outstanding for longer.
terms.short: Scheduled repayment of loan principal over time. A longer period lowers annual Debt Service but leaves principal outstanding for longer.

terms.definition: The recurring costs of running the property, not counting mortgage payments and usually not capital replacements. They are subtracted from revenue to get net operating income, so the assumption directly affects supportable debt.
terms.short: Recurring costs of running the property, excluding mortgage payments and usually capital replacements. They are subtracted from revenue to calculate NOI.

terms.label: Concessions
terms.definition: Temporary incentives such as free rent or reduced move-in costs, used to attract tenants. They lower the revenue collected during lease-up or in a soft market, which can delay stabilization and weaken coverage.
terms.short: Temporary incentives such as free rent or reduced move-in costs. They lower collected revenue during lease-up or a soft market.

terms.label: Stabilization
terms.definition: The point at which a property reaches steady occupancy and operations after lease-up. Lenders and investors test permanent debt and long-term performance against stabilized results, not opening-month results.
terms.short: The point when a property reaches a sustainable occupancy and operating pattern after lease-up. Long-term financing is tested against stabilized results.

terms.definition: A nonprofit that owns land permanently and leases it to the owners of the homes built on it. Because the land is left out of the purchase price, the home costs less. In return, a resale formula limits the sale price to keep the home affordable for the next buyer.
HUD's median family income for an area, the version of area median income used in its CHAS tables. Income groups are described as a percentage of it, such as 80% of HAMFI.

terms.label: Ground lease
terms.definition: An arrangement in which the buyer owns the house and leases the land under it, long term, from a community land trust, housing authority or town. The buyer pays a small monthly land fee, and the lease sets the rules for resale.

terms.label: Deed restriction
terms.definition: A legal limit recorded on a property's deed. On affordable for-sale homes it usually caps the resale price and requires the next buyer to meet an income limit, while the owner still owns both house and land.
terms.short: A legal restriction on a property's title that locks in affordability by capping rent or sale price. It survives changes of ownership.

terms.label: Covenant
terms.definition: A recorded promise tied to a property that binds current and future owners, such as a limit on resale price or on who can buy. It works much like a deed restriction.

terms.label: Net proceeds
terms.definition: The money a seller keeps after paying selling costs, the mortgage balance and anything owed back to public programs.

terms.label: Recapture
terms.definition: Repayment of public homebuyer assistance when a home is sold, so that the money can help another buyer. Programs use it alone or together with a capped resale price.
Census Bureau data on where people work and where workers live, down to the census block. This site uses it for local jobs, wages and commuting.
terms.short: LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics — federal commuter-flow data used to map where workers live versus where they work.

terms.definition: The part of LODES that counts jobs by where the job is located, broken down by wage band and industry.
The part of LODES that links each worker's home area to their work area. It is used to measure commuting into and out of a place.
The standard codes used to group businesses and jobs by industry, such as construction or health care.
Colorado's official source of population and household estimates and forecasts. It is part of DOLA.
terms.short: State Demography Office — Colorado state office within DOLA producing population, housing-unit, and labor-force estimates and projections by county and place.

terms.full: Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income
terms.definition: A Census measure of the share of a renter household's income that goes to gross rent, meaning rent plus the utilities and fuels the renter pays. Paying more than 30% is HUD's definition of cost burdened.
HUD's yearly income limits for LIHTC and tax-exempt bond housing. They set who qualifies for the homes and, through the Section 42 rent formula, the maximum rents.
terms.short: Multifamily Tax Subsidy Projects — HUD's yearly income limits for LIHTC and tax-exempt bond projects. They set the maximum rent allowed at each AMI tier.

source.name: HUD Multifamily Tax Subsidy Project Income Limits

terms.definition: The Census Bureau's count of new homes authorized by building permits. It is published for the nation, states, metro areas, counties and permit-issuing places.
terms.short: Census Building Permits Survey — the federal count of new homes authorized by building permits, by state, metro area, county and place.

terms.definition: The state housing agency, part of DOLA. It funds affordable housing and runs state housing programs.
terms.short: Colorado Division of Housing — the state agency within DOLA that funds and regulates affordable housing.

terms.definition: A local agency that runs public housing, housing vouchers, or both, under HUD rules.
A housing voucher tied to specific homes in a building instead of to a tenant, so the rent help stays with the building.
terms.short: Project-Based Voucher — federal rental assistance tied to specific units (not a tenant). Gives the project a stable rent stream that supports deeper affordability.

terms.full: HUD Office of Public and Indian Housing
terms.definition: The HUD office that oversees public housing agencies and the housing voucher programs.
The Fair Housing Act duty of HUD-funded jurisdictions to take active steps against segregation and to widen housing choice.

Zillow's index of asking rents, built from homes listed for rent on Zillow more than once. It averages the middle of the market, the 35th to 65th percentile, and usually runs ahead of Census rents, which include long-time tenants.
terms.short: Zillow Observed Rent Index — Zillow's asking-rent index for the middle of the market (35th to 65th percentile). Free monthly downloads at zillow.com/research.

terms.definition: Zillow's estimate of the typical home value in an area.
The federal agency that oversees Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks. It publishes the House Price Index.
terms.short: Federal Housing Finance Agency — regulates Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Home Loan Banks, and publishes the House Price Index (HPI) used to track home-price changes by state and metro.

terms.definition: FHFA's measure of how single-family home prices change over time. It is built from repeat sales and refinancings of the same homes with Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac mortgages.
terms.short: House Price Index — FHFA's quarterly measure of single-family home price change, computed from repeat-sales transactions on conforming-conventional mortgages.

terms.definition: Federal tax law. Its Section 42 creates the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit and its rent formula.
A bill that started in the Colorado House of Representatives. Bills are numbered by year, as in HB 24-1434.
The statewide association of real estate agents. It publishes monthly reports on home sales, prices and inventory.
Shorthand for households. A household is all the people who live together in one home.
Shorthand for multifamily: buildings with several homes in them, such as apartments.
Grants or loans that help a homebuyer cover the down payment, and sometimes closing costs.
A federal tax credit for part of the mortgage interest a qualifying homebuyer pays each year.
A city agency that can use tax increment financing and land write-downs to support redevelopment, including housing.
A local rule that requires or encourages new developments to include some affordable homes.
terms.short: Inclusionary Zoning — a local policy requiring or encouraging affordable units in new market-rate residential development.

terms.full: Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008
terms.definition: A 2008 federal law. Its HERA Special income limits are higher limits that HUD publishes only for tax credit projects in service in 2007 or 2008 in qualifying areas.
terms.short: Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 — federal law behind the HERA Special income limits, which HUD publishes only for LIHTC projects in service in 2007 or 2008.

source.name: HUD Multifamily Tax Subsidy Project Income Limits

terms.definition: Net operating income divided by the year's loan payments. A ratio of 1.15 means income is 15% above the payments. CHFA's 2027–28 QAP requires at least 1.15 on amortized debt through the first 15 years.
terms.short: Debt Service Coverage Ratio — annual NOI divided by annual loan payments. CHFA's 2027–28 QAP requires at least 1.15, meaning income 15% above the payments.

terms.definition: A public fund set aside for affordable housing. It can be local, state or national.
A HUD program of grants to states to build and preserve homes for extremely low-income and very low-income households.
A short, usually non-binding letter stating the intent to go ahead with a deal or a funding application.
A cost per home per year. It is the usual unit for operating expenses.
The investor in a tax credit deal who buys the credits and owns most of the partnership but does not run it.
The developer or sponsor in a tax credit deal that manages the partnership and the property.
A mission-driven lender certified by the U.S. Treasury's CDFI Fund.
The announcement that a funding program is open for applications.
A Colorado tax credit, allocated by CHFA, for rental homes serving households between 80% and 120% AMI, or up to 140% in rural resort counties. Federal credits do not reach these incomes.
terms.short: Middle Income Housing Tax Credit — a Colorado state program for households between 80% and 120% AMI (workforce: teachers, nurses, first responders).

terms.definition: Affordable housing paired with support services, usually for people who have experienced homelessness or live with a disability.
A nonprofit certified to receive the share of federal HOME funds set aside for community groups.
HUD rental vouchers for veterans who have experienced homelessness, paired with VA case management.
An agreed payment a property makes in place of regular property taxes. For an affordable project it is usually a reduced, fixed amount, which lowers operating costs.
terms.short: Payment in Lieu of Taxes — an agreement under which an affordable project pays a reduced, fixed amount instead of normal property taxes. Lowers operating costs.

terms.definition: A recorded agreement that keeps a property's rents and tenant incomes restricted for a set number of years.
Households at or below 30% of area median income. HUD's own extremely low-income limit is the higher of 30% of the median and the federal poverty guideline.
Colorado's constitutional limit on how much revenue the state can keep and spend.
The public transit agency for the Denver area.
The standard format transit agencies use to publish routes, stops and schedules.
The state transportation agency. This site uses its traffic counts and transit data when screening sites.
terms.short: Colorado Department of Transportation — state agency publishing traffic counts and transit data used in site-suitability analysis.

terms.definition: Areas where homes meet or mix with undeveloped wildland. Wildfire risk is higher there.
FEMA's high-risk flood zone: land with at least a 1% chance of flooding in any given year.
A free, crowd-sourced world map. This site uses it for amenities such as grocery stores and schools.

terms.full: Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing
terms.definition: The Census Bureau's map files of boundaries such as states, counties, places and census tracts.
terms.short: Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing — the Census Bureau's geographic boundary files (states, counties, tracts, places).

terms.definition: Local approval to use a site in a way the zoning allows only under conditions, often after a public hearing.
The USDA agency that finances housing in rural areas. Its programs include Section 515 rental loans, Section 538 loan guarantees and Section 502 home loans.
terms.short: USDA Rural Development — federal financing programs (Section 515 / 538 / 502) supporting affordable rental and owner-occupied housing in rural communities.

terms.definition: The federal department whose Rural Development agency finances rural housing.
The federal disaster agency. It publishes the flood zone maps.
The federal environmental agency. This site uses its Smart Location Database for walkability and transit access.
Flexible HUD funding, granted each year by formula to states and to larger cities and counties, for housing rehabilitation, homebuyer help, infrastructure and other community projects.
terms.short: Community Development Block Grant — a flexible annual HUD formula grant to states and large cities for affordable-housing rehab, homebuyer assistance, infrastructure and other community development.

terms.definition: A HUD program that converts public housing to long-term project-based rental assistance so that it can be refinanced and repaired.
A federally defined metro area: a core city plus the counties tied to it by commuting.
The shared database real estate agents use to list homes for sale and record sales.

Housing within a ½-mile walk of frequent public transit. CHFA's 2027–28 QAP (§5.B.2.b) gives 5 points to a project at an existing or planned transit-oriented (TOD or TOC) site, up from 3 in the 2025–26 QAP.
terms.short: Transit-Oriented Development — projects within a ½-mile walk of transit. Earns 5 CHFA QAP points under the adopted 2027–28 QAP (§5.B.2.b), which also counts TOC sites; the 2025–26 QAP gave 3.

terms.definition: The federal law requiring an environmental review before federal funds are used on a project.
A HUD block grant to states and local governments to build, buy or repair homes for low-income households, or to help them with rent.
terms.short: HOME Investment Partnerships Program — annual HUD formula grant funding affordable-housing acquisition, new construction, rehab, and tenant rental assistance.

terms.full: Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design
terms.definition: A widely used green building certification.
A tax credit for rehabilitating certified historic buildings. The federal credit is 20% of qualified rehabilitation costs, and Colorado has its own state credit.

The competitive federal housing credit. It is worth about 70% of a building's eligible cost in present value. Each state gets a limited amount per year, so projects compete through a scored CHFA application.
terms.short: 9% LIHTC — the competitive federal credit. Worth about 70% of a building's eligible cost in present value, but states only get a limited annual allocation, so projects compete through a scored CHFA application.

terms.definition: The federal housing credit that comes with tax-exempt bond financing instead of the scored competition. It is worth about 30% of a building's eligible cost in present value and is available year-round, subject to the state's bond cap.
terms.short: 4% LIHTC — the non-competitive federal credit, paired with tax-exempt bonds. Worth about 30% of a building's eligible cost in present value. Available year-round subject to a state bond cap.

source.name: 26 U.S.C. 42, Low-income housing credit, subsections (b)(1) and (h)(4)

terms.label: Rent burden
terms.definition: A renter household paying more than 30% of income for rent and utilities. Above 50% is severe rent burden. It is HUD's standard measure of affordability stress.
terms.short: A renter paying more than 30% of gross income on rent and utilities. Over 50% is "severely rent-burdened." HUD's standard measure of affordability stress.

terms.label: Cost burden
terms.definition: A household, renting or owning, paying more than 30% of income for housing including utilities. Above 50% is severe cost burden. It is HUD's standard affordability measure for both renters and owners.
terms.short: Renters or owners spending more than 30% of income on housing (rent or mortgage plus utilities). Over 50% is "severely cost-burdened." HUD's standard affordability measure for both tenure types.

terms.label: Absorption
terms.definition: How fast a market leases newly built homes, in homes per month. It is used to project lease-up time and size the construction loan, and slow absorption signals weak demand.
terms.short: How fast a market leases up newly built units, expressed as units per month. Used to project lease-up time and size the construction loan; slow absorption signals weak demand.

terms.label: Market study
terms.definition: A third-party report testing whether a project has enough qualifying renters at reasonable rents. LIHTC applications and most lenders require one, and a CHFA application needs a CHFA-approved analyst.
terms.short: A third-party report, by a CHFA-approved analyst for CHFA applications, testing whether a project has enough qualifying renters and reasonable rents. Required for LIHTC and by most lenders; a weak study can kill a deal.

terms.definition: A 2022 Colorado ballot measure setting aside state income tax revenue equal to up to 0.1% of taxable income (estimated at $290M a year from 2023-24) for affordable housing: 60% to OEDIT's Affordable Housing Financing Fund (run by CHFA), 40% to DOLA. For most of the money (homelessness programs and modular-manufacturer loans are exempt), the local government must file a commitment with DOLA: 3% growth a year for 2024–2026, then a permit-based goal from 2027.
terms.short: A 2022 Colorado ballot measure setting aside state income tax revenue equal to up to 0.1% of taxable income (estimated at $290M a year from 2023-24) for affordable housing: 60% to OEDIT's Affordable Housing Financing Fund (run by CHFA), 40% to DOLA. For most of the money (homelessness programs and modular-manufacturer loans are exempt), the local government must file a commitment with DOLA: 3% growth a year for 2024–2026, then a permit-based goal from 2027.

terms.definition: Colorado's state Affordable Housing Tax Credit, which CHFA allocates alongside the federal credit. A full six-year allocation of state credit equals 30% of qualified basis for new construction and rehabilitation.
terms.short: Colorado's state Affordable Housing Tax Credit, allocated by CHFA alongside the federal credit. A full six-year allocation equals 30% of qualified basis.

terms.label: Soft debt
terms.definition: A loan with below-market interest, deferred payments, or repayment only from project cash flow. Cities, counties and Prop 123 programs use it to fill financing gaps.
terms.short: A loan with below-market interest, deferred payments, or repayment only from project cash flow. Cities, counties, and Prop 123 use it to fill financing gaps.

terms.label: Linkage fee
terms.definition: A fee on new commercial or market-rate residential development, charged per square foot and paid into an affordable housing fund.
terms.short: A fee on new commercial or market-rate residential development, paid into an affordable housing fund. Set per square foot.

terms.label: Capture rate
terms.definition: The share of income-qualified renters in a market area a proposed project needs to lease its units. CHFA counts renters whose income fits the unit's AMI limit and who would pay no more than 40% of income in rent, and its 2027–28 QAP will not accept capture above 85% without more demand data.
terms.short: The share of income-qualified renters in a market area a proposed project needs to lease its units. CHFA counts renters whose income fits the unit's AMI limit and who would pay no more than 40% of income in rent, and its 2027–28 QAP will not accept capture above 85% without more demand data.

terms.definition: The standard code the Census Bureau gives every state, county, place and tract. It keeps data joined correctly across sources.
terms.short: The standard federal identifier the Census Bureau uses to keep data joined cleanly across sources. Every county or place has a unique GEOID.

terms.definition: The practice of checking that data inputs are current, complete and consistent across sources before any conclusion is drawn.
terms.short: Quality Assurance / Quality Control — the discipline of verifying that data inputs are current, complete, and reconcile across sources before any conclusion is drawn.

terms.full: FRED series ID for FHFA's Colorado House Price Index
terms.definition: A quarterly repeat-sales index of Colorado home prices, published by FHFA. COSTHPI is its series ID on FRED, where it can be downloaded at fred.stlouisfed.org.
terms.short: FRED series ID for FHFA's Colorado House Price Index — the quarterly repeat-sales index for Colorado, downloadable from FRED at fred.stlouisfed.org.

terms.definition: The federal agency that publishes the Consumer Price Index, employment data and wage statistics.
terms.short: Bureau of Labor Statistics — the federal agency that publishes the Consumer Price Index (CPI), employment data, and wage statistics.

terms.definition: The federal agency that publishes gross domestic product, personal income and regional economic accounts.
terms.short: Bureau of Economic Analysis — the federal agency that publishes Gross Domestic Product (GDP), personal income, and regional economic accounts.

terms.definition: The federal tax agency. It administers the LIHTC rules in Section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code.
terms.short: Internal Revenue Service — the federal tax authority. For affordable housing, IRS administers the LIHTC program rules under Section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code.

terms.definition: The part of HUD that insures mortgages. Its multifamily programs, Section 221(d)(4) and Section 223(f), back loans to build and refinance rental housing.
terms.short: Federal Housing Administration — HUD division that insures multifamily mortgage loans (221(d)(4), 223(f)) used for affordable housing construction and refinance.

terms.definition: A company chartered by Congress to support housing finance: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks. They finance affordable housing through LIHTC equity and below-market loans.
terms.short: Government-Sponsored Enterprise — Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks. They finance affordable housing through LIHTC equity and below-market debt.

terms.definition: A federal law requiring lenders to report mortgage applications, loans and denials by census tract. Its data is the standard source for studying access to mortgage credit.
terms.short: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act — federal law requiring lenders to report loan origination and denial data by census tract; the canonical source for mortgage-credit access analysis.

terms.definition: Another name for housing tax credits. Some states use it for the federal LIHTC program, and others for a state credit layered on top.
terms.short: Affordable Housing Tax Credit — alternate name some states use for the federal LIHTC program (or for layered state credits).

terms.full: National Council of Housing Market Analysts
terms.definition: The industry body that publishes professional standards for LIHTC market studies, covering capture rates, comparable properties and demand calculations.
terms.short: National Council of Housing Market Analysts — the industry body that publishes professional standards for LIHTC market studies (capture-rate methodology, comparable selection, demand calculations).

terms.definition: The standard measure of total economic output. This site tracks state GDP from the Bureau of Economic Analysis.
terms.short: Gross Domestic Product — the standard measure of total economic output. This site tracks state GDP from the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

terms.definition: The ACS table of median gross rent for a census tract or place. It is the most direct free rent figure for a single place.
terms.short: ACS table B25064 — median gross rent by census tract or place. The cleanest free per-place rent figure available.

terms.definition: The ACS table of vacant homes by the reason they are vacant. It is used to compute a vacancy rate for a tract.
terms.short: ACS table B25004 — vacant housing units by reason vacant. Used to compute vacancy rate at tract level.

terms.definition: The ACS table of tenure: homes occupied by owners and homes occupied by renters, by census tract.
terms.short: ACS table B25003 — tenure (owner vs. renter occupied) by census tract.

terms.definition: The ACS table of gross rent as a percentage of household income. It shows how rent burden is distributed in a tract.
terms.short: ACS table B25070 — gross rent as a percentage of household income (rent-burden distribution) by tract.

terms.definition: The ACS table of household income for all households. The AMI gap model keeps it as its older all-household series and population proxy.
terms.short: ACS table B19001 — household income distribution (all tenures). Retained as the AMI-gap model's legacy all-household series and population proxy.

terms.definition: The ACS table of tenure by household income. Its renter rows are the demand side of the AMI gap model: renter households in each AMI band.
terms.short: ACS table B25118 — tenure by household income. The renter-household bins are the AMI-gap model's demand side: renter households at each AMI band.

terms.definition: The ACS table of median household income, by census tract.
terms.short: ACS table B19013 — median household income by census tract.

terms.definition: The loan amount divided by total development cost. Lenders use it to size construction loans.
terms.short: Loan-to-Cost — the ratio of mortgage debt to total development cost (TDC). Used in construction-loan sizing.

terms.definition: A home restricted to rent or sell for less than the market price, usually through a deed restriction, inclusionary zoning or a covenant.
terms.short: Below Market Rate — a unit restricted to rent or sell at less than market price, usually via deed restriction, inclusionary zoning, or covenant.

terms.definition: A commercial real estate services firm. Its Multifamily Outlook publishes Denver-area rent, vacancy and concession data each quarter.
terms.short: CBRE — a global commercial real-estate services firm whose Multifamily Outlook publishes Denver-area rent, vacancy, and concession data quarterly.

terms.definition: A real estate data company. Its Foreclosure Activity Report tracks default, auction and bank-owned filings by metro area.
terms.short: ATTOM Data Solutions — a real-estate data aggregator whose Foreclosure Activity Report tracks default, auction, and bank-owned filings by metro.

terms.definition: A subscription database of commercial real estate. It tracks rent, vacancy, sales and the construction pipeline by submarket.
terms.short: CoStar — a paid commercial real-estate data subscription tracking rent, vacancy, sales comps, and pipeline by submarket.

terms.definition: The apartment industry's trade group for metro Denver. Its quarterly Vacancy and Rent Survey is the standard read on Denver-area apartment performance.
terms.short: Apartment Association of Metro Denver — the trade group whose quarterly Vacancy & Rent Survey is the standard read on Denver-area apartment performance.

terms.full: Colorado Department of Labor and Employment
terms.definition: The state agency that publishes unemployment, wage and labor force data by county.
terms.short: Colorado Department of Labor and Employment — state agency publishing unemployment, wage, and labor-force data by county.

terms.full: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment
terms.definition: The state agency that tracks environmental and public health indicators. This site uses them in site screening.
terms.short: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment — state agency tracking environmental and public-health indicators used in site-screening.

terms.definition: The regional housing authority that served Gunnison County and Crested Butte. Its work has moved to the Gunnison County Housing Authority, whose pages now answer at gvrha.org.
terms.short: Gunnison Valley Regional Housing Authority — the regional housing authority that served Gunnison County and Crested Butte. Its work has moved to the Gunnison County Housing Authority.

terms.definition: The housing authority for Aspen and Pitkin County. It runs Aspen's deed-restricted workforce housing program.
terms.short: Aspen Pitkin County Housing Authority — the resort-area housing authority that operates Aspen's deed-restricted workforce-housing program.

terms.definition: The regional housing authority serving Telluride and Mountain Village.
terms.short: San Miguel Regional Housing Authority — the regional housing authority serving Telluride and Mountain Village.

terms.definition: The regional housing authority serving Steamboat Springs and the rest of Routt County.
terms.short: Yampa Valley Housing Authority — the regional housing authority serving Steamboat Springs and surrounding Routt County.

terms.definition: HUD's rental assistance program. It includes Housing Choice Vouchers, which move with the tenant, and Project-Based Vouchers, which stay with the home.
terms.short: HUD's federal rental-assistance program. Includes Housing Choice Vouchers (tenant-based) and Project-Based Vouchers (unit-based).

terms.full: Section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code
terms.definition: The federal law that creates the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit and sets its rules on basis, income limits, rent caps and compliance.
terms.short: Section 42 of the federal Internal Revenue Code — the law that creates the LIHTC program and defines its rules (basis, income limits, rent caps, compliance).

terms.definition: A USDA Rural Development program of low-interest loans for affordable rental housing in rural areas. Properties often combine it with LIHTC equity.
terms.short: USDA Rural Development Section 515 — low-interest loans for affordable rental housing in rural areas. Often combined with LIHTC equity.

terms.definition: A USDA Rural Development program that guarantees private loans for affordable rental housing in rural areas.
terms.short: USDA Rural Development Section 538 — loan guarantee program supporting privately financed rural affordable rental housing.

terms.definition: An FHA mortgage insurance program for building or substantially rehabilitating multifamily rental housing.
terms.short: FHA mortgage insurance program for new construction or substantial rehabilitation of multifamily rental housing.

terms.definition: An FHA mortgage insurance program for buying or refinancing existing multifamily rental properties.
terms.short: FHA mortgage insurance program for acquisition or refinance of existing multifamily rental properties.

terms.definition: This site's 0–100 reading of how well a market supports new affordable rentals at a chosen site. It is the weighted sum of five parts: Demand 30%, Competitive Density 25%, Rent Pressure 15%, Market Tightness 15% and Workforce 15%. Scores of 80 or more read Strong, 60–79 Moderate, 40–59 Marginal and under 40 Weak. It is not a CHFA score.

source.name: This site's Market Analysis scoring notes

terms.label: Competitive density
terms.definition: A part of this site's PMA score, 25% of the total, that reads how crowded a market area already is. It divides the income-restricted homes already there by the renter households who qualify for them. No such homes scores 100, and the score falls to 0 when they reach 85% of those renters, the level CHFA's 2027–28 QAP questions.

source.name: This site's Market Analysis scoring code

terms.label: Rent pressure
terms.definition: A part of this site's PMA score, 15% of the total, that compares the market area's median rent with the rent a household at 60% of the county's AMI can afford at 30% of income. Median rent at 70% of that affordable rent or less scores 0, and at 150% or more scores 100.

source.name: This site's Market Analysis scoring code

terms.label: Market tightness
terms.definition: A part of this site's PMA score, 15% of the total, read from the rental vacancy rate after for-rent homes in seasonal markets are discounted. No vacancy scores 100, and vacancy of 10% or more scores 0. A tight market suggests new homes will lease quickly.

source.name: This site's Market Analysis scoring notes

terms.definition: A part of this site's PMA score, 30% of the total, shown there as Demand. It reads how much unmet need for affordable rentals a market area shows by blending four measures: the share of renters who are cost burdened (45%), the share severely cost burdened (20%), the poverty rate (10%) and the renter share of households (25%).

source.name: This site's Market Analysis scoring code

terms.definition: A part of this site's PMA score, 15% of the total, shown there as Workforce. Two inputs are measured today: the balance of jobs and homes in the market area, from Census LODES, and local household income against the county's AMI. Three more planned inputs are left out until real data exist, and the tool says so.

source.name: This site's Market Analysis scoring notes

terms.label: Competitive supply share
terms.definition: A proposed project's share of the competing affordable homes it would lease up against: its homes divided by those homes plus the competing ones on record. It is not a capture rate, which divides by renter households. This site shows it from observed records only and gives no risk rating while that inventory is incomplete.

source.name: This site's Market Analysis scoring notes

terms.label: Housing needs fit
terms.definition: A check on this site's deal concept card of how well a proposed mix of homes matches local need. It compares the homes planned at 30%, 50% and 60% AMI with the homes needed at each level and averages the three coverage shares: 50% or more reads strong, 15–49% partial and less than that weak.

terms.label: Housing needs scorecard
terms.definition: This site's 0–100 reading of a place's housing need. It averages up to four percentile ranks: cost burden, the share of lower-income renters at 30% AMI or below, renters paying over half their income, and home price against income. The last is always the county's rank. A place with fewer than 50 renter households uses its county's for all four.

source.name: This site's method note on the Housing Needs Assessment page

terms.label: Overall need score
terms.definition: This site's 0–100 ranking index for a county, town or CDP: 55% community need and 45% opportunity. Need blends the housing gap, cost burden, affordability, future pressure and overcrowding. Opportunity blends economic mobility, walkability, amenities and QCT or DDA status. Nearly every input is a percentile among places of the same type, so the score is relative.

terms.label: AMI gap
terms.definition: The rental homes priced for households at or below an AMI level minus the renter households at or below it, for a county or place. A negative number is a shortage. This site computes it from Census ACS rents and renter incomes against HUD income limits, and it does not test whether those homes are available to rent.

terms.label: Affordable ownership need
terms.definition: A screening view on this site's needs assessment pages with two parts: the shortfall of rental homes priced for renter households at or below 80% AMI, and the pool of renter households at 51–100% of HUD's median family income who might buy. The pool is not a count of mortgage-ready buyers.

source.name: This site's method note on the Housing Needs Assessment page

terms.label: Market health composite
terms.definition: This site's 0–100 reading of a county's economy and mortgage market. It averages five percentile ranks among Colorado's 64 counties, equally weighted: the five-year change in employed residents, five-year population growth, unemployment (inverted), mortgage originations per 1,000 households and the mortgage denial rate (inverted). Higher means a stronger market.

source.name: This site's method note on the Colorado Deep Dive page

terms.label: Housing outcome score
terms.definition: This site's 0–100 summary of a deal on the Deal Calculator. It weights four parts: how much of the local affordability gap the homes cover (30%), local policy support (20%), financial feasibility (30%) and site quality (20%). It fills in as each step is completed and carries a letter grade, with A at 85 and above.

terms.label: Civic readiness
terms.definition: A part of this site's Opportunity Finder score that counts the local housing tools a place has on record, up to seven: a housing needs assessment, a Prop 123 commitment, a housing authority, housing nonprofits, a comprehensive plan, an inclusionary zoning ordinance and local funding. A place with no record of its own uses its county's.

source.name: This site's housing policy scorecard data
